query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The evolution of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy from a metastable state to a more stable state, through the formation of intermetallic compounds and solid solutions, changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior due to the transformation of its microstructure and the resulting changes in its constituent properties.

generation.predicted_outcome: 20% decrease in corrosion rate and 15% decrease in high-temperature oxidation rate compared to the initial baseline
generation.baseline: As-cast alloy with a corrosion rate of 0.5 mm/year and a high-temperature oxidation rate of 1.2 mm/year
generation.uncertainty: The exact transformation pathways and the resulting changes in microstructure and constituent properties are not well understood and may vary depending on the specific alloy composition and processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior of the as-cast alloy and the annealed alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion rate and high-temperature oxidation rate of the annealed alloy are not significantly different from those of the as-cast alloy (i.e., less than 5% decrease), the hypothesis is falsified
